chapters.title: Chapter 2: Price Formation, Spreads and Liquidity

lessons.title: Case Study: Spread and Depth Behavior in a Liquid Large Cap vs an Illiquid Small Cap

body.text: Two stocks can trade under the exact same exchange rules, the same tick size, the same price-time priority, and still behave like they belong to entirely different markets. The three-component spread framework from this chapter explains why, in detail specific enough to act on.

children.text: Two Stocks, Same Rules, Different Worlds

Consider two illustrative NSE-listed stocks trading on an ordinary day. Stock L is a Nifty 50-style large cap with heavy institutional and retail interest. Stock S is a small cap outside the Nifty 500 with a real business and a real listing, but comparatively little daily trading interest. Both trade under the same ₹0.05 tick size, the same price-time priority rules, and the same exchange infrastructure covered in this chapter. What differs entirely is how many participants show up to compete for the trade, and that single difference cascades through every concept this chapter has built.

children.text: The Intraday Spread Pattern, and Why Both Stocks Share Its Shape

Spreads across most equity markets, NSE included, follow a well-documented U-shape over the trading day: wider near the open, tightest through the middle of the session, and wider again near the close. Both Stock L and Stock S follow this pattern, but the small cap's swing is disproportionately larger.

body.title: Illustrative Intraday Spread Pattern, in Ticks

body.text: The chart above is a stylized illustration built to match the well-documented U-shape of intraday spreads, not observed tick data for any specific stock. The exact widening ratio between a given large cap and small cap will vary by name and by day.

children.text: The open widens for both stocks because overnight news, global cues, and anything that happened since the previous close all land on the market at once, raising the adverse selection risk any liquidity provider faces from Lesson 1's framework. The close widens for a related reason: positioning ahead of the next session, index rebalancing flows, and the closing auction mechanics all raise the odds that the next order in is informed rather than routine. Stock L's competing liquidity providers from Lesson 2 pull that widening back down quickly once the open settles, because enough of them are competing for the trade that any one participant's overly wide quote gets undercut almost immediately. Stock S has no such competitive pressure; with only one or two participants willing to quote at all, a wide opening spread has far less pulling it back toward normal, and normal itself is already many ticks wide to begin with.

children.text: Why This Matters Before You Point a Signal at Either Stock

This case study is not just a liquidity comparison, it is a preview of a mistake Chapter 3 and Chapter 4 are built to help you avoid. Signals like order flow imbalance and order book imbalance work by reading shifts in adverse selection risk from the book itself, which assumes there is enough competitive two-sided flow for those shifts to be meaningful. On Stock L, where adverse selection is genuinely the dominant, time-varying component of the spread, that assumption largely holds. On Stock S, where order processing and inventory costs dominate a spread that barely moves day to day regardless of information flow, the same signal computed the same way is reading mostly noise, one or two participants' inventory management, not a genuine shift in informed trading risk. A backtest that does not separate these two regimes can show a signal working on average across a universe of stocks while actually working only on the liquid names and quietly failing on the illiquid ones.

body.text: Never backtest a microstructure signal across a mixed universe of liquid and illiquid names without checking whether it works on each group separately. A signal built on adverse selection dynamics can look profitable on average while its entire edge comes from a handful of liquid stocks, masked by noise on everything else.

body.title: Identifying the Stock From the Book Alone
body.scenario: Two anonymized NSE-listed stocks, X and Y. Stock X: best bid 4,800 shares at ₹612.40, best ask 5,100 shares at ₹612.45, roughly 42,000 shares of depth across the top five levels, and over 30,000 trades printed by midday. Stock Y: best bid 150 shares at ₹88.10, best ask 90 shares at ₹89.60, roughly 900 shares of depth across the top five levels, and about 40 trades printed by midday.
body.prompt: Which stock is more likely the liquid large cap and which the illiquid small cap? Point to at least two specific pieces of evidence from the snapshot, using this chapter's framework, that support your answer.
body.modelAnswer: Stock X is almost certainly the liquid large cap. Its spread is exactly ₹0.05, one tick, consistent with many competing liquidity providers narrowing the market to the minimum possible spread, as in Lesson 2's picture of voluntary competition. Its best-price depth is in the thousands of shares on each side and its trade count is high by midday, both consistent with a crowded, actively quoted book. Stock Y is almost certainly the illiquid small cap. Its spread of ₹1.50 is roughly 30 ticks, consistent with order processing and inventory costs dominating in a thinly traded name from Lesson 1's framework, and its depth of under 150 to 200 shares per side plus very low trade count both point to few or no competing participants, closer to the mandated single market maker scenario from Lesson 2 than to a competitive large-cap book.

body.title: Why Spreads Widen at the Open and Close, Even Without News
body.question: Why do spreads on both a liquid large cap and an illiquid small cap typically widen near the market open and again near the close, even on an ordinary day with no specific company news?
options: Exchange transaction charges are higher during the first and last minutes of trading
Uncertainty about overnight information at the open, and positioning ahead of the next session near the close, both raise adverse selection risk for liquidity providers
Tick size automatically increases during the opening and closing windows
Liquidity providers are contractually required to widen quotes during these specific windows
body.explanation: The U-shaped intraday spread pattern is an adverse selection story, not a fee or a rule change. At the open, overnight news and global cues create genuine uncertainty about where informed flow might be positioned. Near the close, index rebalancing and next-session positioning raise the same risk. Liquidity providers respond the only way they rationally can, by widening the compensation they demand for the risk of trading against someone who knows more, exactly as covered in Lesson 1.

points: Identical exchange rules produce very different order books once the number of competing liquidity providers differs, as this chapter's large cap vs small cap comparison shows directly

Spreads follow a U-shape across the trading day on both liquid and illiquid stocks, driven by adverse selection risk rising at the open and close, but the swing is proportionally far larger on thin names

On a liquid stock, adverse selection is the dominant, time-varying component of the spread; on an illiquid stock, order processing and inventory costs dominate a spread that stays wide and fairly constant
Effective spread on a meaningful order size can differ by more than an order of magnitude between a liquid large cap and an illiquid small cap under identical exchange rules
A handful of concrete numbers from an order book snapshot, spread in ticks, depth at the touch, and trade count, are usually enough to correctly classify a stock's liquidity regime

Microstructure signals that read adverse selection dynamics need enough competitive two-sided flow to be meaningful, and backtesting them across mixed liquid and illiquid universes without separating the two can hide a signal that only actually works on the liquid names
